sections.title: The Hook: From Scalar Growth to System Growth
sections.content: Begin with the familiar scalar differential equation dy/dt = ay, where the solution is y(t) = e^{at}. Introduce the concept that systems of objects (like populations or circuits) interact simultaneously. Transition to the matrix form dV/dt = AV, and pose the question: Can we simply 'raise e' to a matrix power?
sections.example: Imagine a digital 'Slime Mold' character. If it grows at a rate 'a', its size is e^{at}. If we have two species of Slime Molds that eat each other's nutrients, we need a matrix to describe their shared growth.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Taylor Series Bridge
sections.content: Recall the Taylor Series expansion for the scalar e^x = 1 + x + x^2/2! + x^3/3! + ... This is the 'DNA' of the exponential function. Since matrices can be added, multiplied, and scaled, we can plug a square matrix A into this exact same infinite blueprint.
sections.example: Visualizing a 'Mathematical Blender': Feed in the scalar 'x' to get a number; feed in the matrix 'A' (using the Identity matrix I instead of 1) to get a new matrix.

sections.title: The Formal Definition of e^A
sections.content: Define e^A = I + A + (A^2)/2! + (A^3)/3! + ... Emphasize that the result of a matrix exponential is always another matrix of the same size. Explain that while the sum is infinite, it always converges for any square matrix.
sections.example: Show a 2x2 matrix A. Calculate the first three terms of the series (I, A, and A^2/2) and show how they sum up to approximate the final transformation matrix.

sections.title: Visualizing the Transformation (The Vector Field)
sections.content: Use a 2D coordinate grid. If a vector represents the state of a system (e.g., Robot position and velocity), e^{At} acts as a 'flow operator.' As time 't' increases, the matrix e^{At} smoothly warps and rotates the grid, carrying the vector along the trajectory of the differential equation.
sections.example: An animation of a circular grid stretching into an ellipse as time progresses, showing how an initial point (Robot start) follows a path determined by matrix A.

sections.title: The Shortcut: Diagonalization
sections.content: Explain that computing infinite sums is hard. Introduce the 'Eigen-shortcut': If A = PDP^-1, then e^A = P e^D P^-1. Since D is diagonal, e^D is simply the exponential of each diagonal element. This is the most efficient way to compute the result.
sections.example: A 'Magic Lens' analogy: The matrix P changes our perspective to a world where components don't interact (diagonal). We grow them easily with e^D, then P^-1 brings us back to the original complicated world.

sections.title: Application: The Predator-Prey Ecosystem
sections.content: Solve a real-world system. Let R be Rabbits and F be Foxes. The interaction is d/dt [R, F] = A [R, F]. Use the matrix exponential e^{At} to predict the population at any time 't'.
sections.example: A simulation graph where e^{At} predicts a oscillating cycle: as Foxes (F) increase, Rabbits (R) decrease, showing how the matrix exponential captures the 'circle of life' in a single mathematical expression.

lecture_lines: Scalar growth follows the exponential function e to the at.
Systems of equations model interacting real-world objects.
Can we raise e to a matrix power instead?

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Taylor Series Bridge
lecture_lines: The Taylor series is the blueprint for exponential functions.
We can plug square matrices into this infinite sum.
Replace the scalar one with the identity matrix I.

storyboard.title: The Formal Definition of e^A
lecture_lines: Define the matrix exponential using the infinite Taylor sum.
Each term adds a power of matrix A.
Factorials ensure the infinite series always converges.
The result is always a matrix of the same size.
This matrix captures the system's entire growth logic.
animations: Write the formal definition e^A = sum(A^n / n!) in #FFFFFF at the top.
Animate the terms I, A, and A^2/2! appearing sequentially in the sum.
Highlight the factorial denominators in #FFD700 (Gold) to emphasize convergence.
Show the summation of these terms into a single 2x2 matrix structure.
Pulse the final matrix in #50C878 (Emerald Green) to represent the captured system logic.

storyboard.title: Visualizing the Transformation (The Vector Field)
lecture_lines: Imagine the system state as a point on a grid.
The matrix exponential acts as a continuous flow operator.
As time passes, the entire grid warps and rotates.
Initial states follow trajectories determined by matrix A.
Watch how the linear transformation evolves over time.
animations: Create a 2D coordinate grid with a distinct point (vector) v in #50C878 (Emerald Green).
Overlay a vector field representing the system dV/dt = AV in #333333.
Animate the grid smoothly warping and rotating as time t increases.
Draw a trailing trajectory line in #FFD700 (Gold) for the vector v.
Display the final transformed grid and vector at a fixed time T.

storyboard.title: The Shortcut: Diagonalization
lecture_lines: Computing infinite sums of matrices is often difficult.
Diagonalization provides a powerful shortcut for calculations.
Perspective changes make the system's components independent.
Exponentiating a diagonal matrix is fast and simple.
Finally, transform back to the original coordinate system.
animations: Display the infinite matrix sum looking complex and difficult to compute.
Introduce the diagonalization shortcut A = PDP^-1 in #50C878 (Emerald Green) alongside the [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/shortcut.svg] icon.
Show the change of basis to the eigen-space where components are independent.
Compute e^D by simply exponentiating the diagonal elements in #FFD700 (Gold).
Transform back to the original basis using P and P^-1 to find e^A.

storyboard.title: Application: The Predator-Prey Ecosystem
lecture_lines: Apply the matrix exponential to a predator-prey system.
The matrix A encodes how species interact and grow.
Solve for future populations using the exponential operator.
animations: Show the Rabbit-Fox system dV/dt = AV where V = [R, F] in #FFFFFF, using the [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/rabbit.svg] icon to represent the rabbit variable.
Highlight the off-diagonal interaction terms in matrix A with #FFD700 (Gold).
Plot the oscillating population curves R(t) and F(t) derived from e^{At}.
